cards.title: Trusting the instrument
cards.body: Today's deck keeps asking one question: can you trust the thing that measures? Gold is moving back home because metal in your own vault is not the same as a promise in someone else's; your watch counts steps but only guesses deep sleep; a compiler can add a backdoor that appears in no line of the source code; and $4 billion of worker monitoring buys stress, not output. The one not to miss is the Alzheimer's piece — a genetic risk score built from European DNA predicted nothing at all in people of African ancestry, while a score built from many ancestries worked. An instrument is only as honest as the people it was built from.

cards.title: India keeps 77% of its gold at home. Europe is moving too.
cards.body: The Reserve Bank of India now keeps 77% of its gold inside India. The Netherlands is moving bullion to London. France has pulled holdings out of New York. Nobody is buying or selling. They are only changing where the gold sits.

sections.text:
Flip that 77% around: close to a quarter of India's gold still sits in vaults abroad.

Europe is making the same move. The Netherlands is shifting its bullion — gold held as bars — to London. France has taken holdings out of New York. The pattern is Europe pulling gold out of US vaults.

The report gives no tonnage. Seventy-seven percent is a share, not a weight. So how much metal has actually travelled, and how fast, we do not know.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 77% — the share of RBI gold now held inside India
About 23% — the rest, still in vaults abroad
Netherlands: bullion moving to London
France: holdings moved out of New York
No weights published — the report names destinations only

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Gold is what a country keeps for its worst day — the asset that still works when currencies, payment systems or trading partners do not. Where it sits only matters on that day. Moving it home means no longer assuming someone else's vault is neutral ground.

recall.q: These central banks are not changing how much gold they hold. What are they changing, and why is that the whole story?
recall.a: They are changing where it sits — India keeps 77% at home, the Netherlands is moving bullion to London, France has pulled holdings out of New York. Gold is the asset a country keeps for its worst day, so moving it home means no longer assuming a foreign vault is neutral ground on that day.

cards.title: A prison sentence: deserved, or a promise to keep?
cards.body: Deterrence, reform, public safety — every purpose we give prison promises something. A man who spent years inside says that makes each sentence a promise, and promises can be broken. The other side answers that punishment is simply owed, like a debt. It promises nothing, so it can fail at nothing.

sections.text:
For a while, David G. Villanueva was not David. He was a number, a cell, a body counted every morning and every evening. He went in with opinions about prison. He came out, he says, with convictions.

He is not against punishment. Societies may protect themselves, and dangerous people sometimes have to be removed — to stop more harm, and to say out loud that some acts cannot be allowed. His question is narrower: what does a sentence owe?

Take the first answer at full strength. Call it honest desert: the punishment is simply what the wrong deserves. A wrong throws the moral world out of balance, and the sentence sets it straight. It is complete the day it ends.

It never promised to repair the man, or to cut next year's crime, or to teach him a trade. It states what the wrong was worth. Ask it for results and you have misread it — you are asking a debt to behave like a medicine. It also protects the prisoner: the term fits the act, not a guess about his future.

Now the second side, also at full strength. Call it the promise. Plato thought punishment should improve the soul of the wrongdoer. Jeremy Bentham said punishment is itself an evil — pain caused on purpose — and is right only if it prevents a greater one.

Both attach a condition. The state is not simply taking years from a person. It takes them in exchange for something: a safer street, a repaired man, a warning others hear. That is a bill it has agreed to pay.

Villanueva stands here, and his charge is sharp. If prison returns people "more damaged, more alienated" — more cut off from others — and no better able to live within the law, that is not a management failure. It is a failure of the idea. The reason given for prison has stopped being true.

So the split is not about facts. It is about which test prison must pass. Desert survives any data, because it promised no outcomes. The promise can be checked. Do fewer people offend again? Do they leave better equipped than they came? Does the place seriously try to learn why people offend at all? Villanueva looked for that effort and did not find it. Name a purpose, he is saying, and you have accepted the test that comes with it.

The two sides do not weigh the same. Modern states do not sell prison as bare desert. They sell protection, deterrence, reform. Foucault suspected prisons were never mainly about reform anyway — that they work as tools of discipline and control, which neither side wants to hear. Three thinkers who agreed on almost nothing each left a standard behind. The test is not whether prison meets your favourite one. It is whether it meets any.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Villanueva's evidence is his own years inside: one man, one system, watched closely. That is testimony, not measurement. It can tell you how the place felt from within. It cannot tell you how often prisons fail, or which ones. The charge does not need that number. It needs only an honest look at whether the promise was ever seriously tried.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A punishment that names its purpose has agreed to be measured by it.

recall.q: When a state defends prison by naming a purpose — safety, deterrence, reform — what does Villanueva say it takes on?
recall.a: A test. A named purpose is a promise, so the sentence can be measured against it: do fewer people offend again, do they leave better equipped. If they leave more damaged and no better able to live within the law, the justification itself has failed, not just the management. Bare desert escapes this, because it promises nothing.

cards.title: Day 7 · The kindness that is really power
cards.body: He forces his way to the brothel to slap Zverkov and finds the room empty — and finds Liza instead. Tonight he discovers he can move another person, and that discovery turns out to be the most dangerous thing that has happened to him yet.

sections.text:
The dark shop, one candle, the familiar drawing-room — and no one in it. They had separated. The slap he borrowed six roubles and paced three hours to deliver arrives at an empty room, and what he feels is relief wearing triumph's clothes: “I felt as though I had been saved from death,” while still insisting, twice, “I should certainly, certainly have given it!” The deed is always safest in the conditional.

Then Liza — pale, grave, “wondering” eyes, and the tell: “I should have hated her if she had been smiling.” Gravity is what he can work with. Something “loathsome” stirs in him; he catches his face in the glass, “pale, angry, abject,” and is glad of it, glad he will seem repulsive to her.

Cut to two o'clock. A clock wheezes behind a screen like something being strangled, the candle end gutters, and the whole day comes back “as though it had been in ambush to pounce upon me again.” Then two open eyes, “coldly detached, sullen,” scrutinising him. The two hours of silence he had found gratifying turn in an instant into the thing he can finally name: vice “revolting as a spider,” which begins with what love ends with. He speaks only to stop the staring.

The interrogation is flat and cruel: name, Riga, tradespeople, a fortnight, twenty. “Why did you leave them?” “Oh, for no reason.” He translates it himself — “That answer meant ‘Let me alone; I feel sick, sad’” — and keeps going anyway. Then the coffin carried up from a Haymarket cellar, the waterlogged graves at Volkovo, “I've seen it myself ... many times.” Parenthesis: he has never been to Volkovo. “A great deal of this was my invention.”

She won't flinch — “Oh, well, then I shall die” — and her refusal to be moved is exactly what escalates him. He switches to arithmetic: a year, a lower house, seven years to a basement. Then to freedom: he can defile himself and walk out, “but you are a slave from the start.”

Then she says “Yes!” — sharp, immediate — and he is thrilled, but not for her: “So she, too, was capable of certain thoughts?” … “it's easy to turn a young soul like that!” And then the sentence that convicts the entire scene: “It was the exercise of my power that attracted me most.” Everything tender that follows runs on top of that.

And it is tender. The stern father kissing his daughter's feet, standing five hours at a party to watch her dance; quarrels that end happily; love as “a holy mystery” hidden from all other eyes; the baby biting the breast and looking sideways as if to say “Look, I am biting!” He gives us both readings in one breath — “It's by pictures, pictures like that one must get at you” and “I did speak with real feeling” — because, as he admits, “cunning so easily goes hand-in-hand with feeling.” Then vanity flares: what if she laughs?

She doesn't laugh. Something soft and shamefaced enters her voice, then hides itself: “you ... speak somehow like a book.” It lands as an insult. Older, he knows what he missed — irony as “the last refuge of modest and chaste-souled people when the privacy of their soul is coarsely and intrusively invaded” — and that her timidity in approaching the sarcasm was the proof. “But I did not guess, and an evil feeling took possession of me. ‘Wait a bit!’”

Chapter VII is the retaliation, and it is expert: you will be scorned, kicked out, abused as though you had beggared her; at twenty-two you will look thirty-five. It ends on the woman turned out on New Year's Day, drunk at nine in the morning, bleeding, beating a salt fish on the stone steps while cabmen taunt her — who was once, perhaps, “fresh as a cherub.” Every word of it is true. None of it is kindness.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: A grim idea came into my brain and passed all over my body, as a horrible sensation, such as one feels when one goes into a damp and mouldy cellar. There was something unnatural in those two eyes, beginning to look at me only now. I recalled, too, that during those two hours I had not said a single word to this creature, and had, in fact, considered it utterly superfluous; in fact, the silence had for some reason gratified me. Now I suddenly realised vividly the hideous idea—revolting as a spider—of vice, which, without love, grossly and shamelessly begins with that in which true love finds its consummation.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: When your kindness needs to be received a certain way, it was never kindness — it was leverage.

recall.q: Liza says he “speak[s] somehow like a book.” Why does that remark turn him cruel?
recall.a: He hears it as mockery of his performance, and his vanity is wounded. Only later does he understand that irony was her defence — “the last refuge of modest and chaste-souled people when the privacy of their soul is coarsely and intrusively invaded” — and that her timidity in bringing herself to say it proved she had been moved. At the time he doesn't guess: “an evil feeling took possession of me. ‘Wait a bit!’” — and he escalates into the pitiless prophecy of Chapter VII.

cards.title: Isolated mice drank more alcohol, and wanted sugar less
cards.body: Eleven days alone made male mice drink more and more alcohol. It also made their brains less interested in sugar. One wire carried the change: from the amygdala, deep in the brain, to the prefrontal cortex at the front. Switch it on and drinking rises. Switch it off and it falls. Female mice, isolated the same way, drank less.
cards.evidence: single study · mice · n=14 male, 11 female · electrophysiology + calcium imaging + optogenetics

sections.text:
Two bottles hang in a mouse's cage. One is plain water. The other is water with 15 percent alcohol. The mouse may drink from either. Move that mouse into a cage of its own for eleven days, and the males start drinking more alcohol, a little more each day.

The easy explanation is that being alone feels bad and alcohol feels good. Two findings do not fit. Female mice, isolated in exactly the same way, drank less. And the isolated males did not want comfort in general: their brains grew more responsive to alcohol and less responsive to sugar water, which mice normally love.

Reesha Patel, Kay Tye and their team had one wire in mind. The basolateral amygdala is an almond-shaped part deep in the brain. It handles emotion and stress. The medial prefrontal cortex sits at the front and weighs things up: decisions, control, what a reward is worth. Cells run straight from the first to the second.

Using tiny glass electrodes — probes that read one cell at a time — they found that isolation made those cells fire more easily in males and less easily in females. The wire moved the way the drinking moved, in both directions.

Then they tested whether the wire was doing the work. Tiny microscopes on the animals' heads showed these cells firing in step with bouts of alcohol drinking, and not with water. The team made the cells sensitive to light, then switched them on every time a mouse licked the spout. Alcohol intake rose, with longer bouts and more licks. Water and sugar water did not change. Turning the wire on in mice who still had cage-mates made their prefrontal cortex act like an isolated animal's — up for alcohol, down for sugar. Turning it off in isolated males cut their alcohol bouts and left water untouched.

So isolation is not just a sad background to the drinking. In these males it re-tunes one wire, so alcohol is worth more and ordinary pleasures are worth less. Jun Wang, who was not part of the work, called that link the striking part: a social fact turned into a change in what the brain treats as worth chasing.

What is still unexplained is nearly as interesting. Nobody knows why the same eleven days push females the other way, and the on-off tests were run only in males. Rank mattered too: lower-ranking mice of both sexes were already drinking more before any isolation began. And these animals were put in single cages by a scientist. That is not the same thing as loneliness.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Fourteen males and eleven females — small groups, though normal for this kind of work. The setup measures drinking that climbs, not addiction. Nothing here tests compulsive drinking, drinking despite harm, or withdrawal. So Wang's warning holds: "isolation causes alcohol use disorder" is a step beyond the data. Patel adds that shutting a mouse in a cage alone is not what loneliness feels like to a person. And "males drink more, females do not" describes one mouse strain over about two weeks.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Eleven days changed what a brain counted as worth having. That is a small fact about mice and a large question about us.

recall.q: Isolation could have simply made the mice want any comfort. What in the results shows the change was more specific than that?
recall.a: The isolated males' prefrontal cortex became more responsive to alcohol and less responsive to sugar water. And switching the wire on raised alcohol drinking while water and sugar water stayed flat. The wire changed what counted as worth having, not how much comfort the mice wanted in general.

cards.title: Sugar and touch steer the cells that build your cortex
cards.body: Scientists thought the stem cells that build the human cortex were following a plan held inside themselves. Two new UCLA studies say they read their surroundings instead: how much sugar is around, and a touch from a fibre growing up from deep in the brain. Change either signal and the cell starts making a different kind of neuron.
cards.evidence: two studies · donated human tissue plus stem-cell organoids and assembloids · sample sizes not given

sections.text:
You are a single cell, long and thin, stretched from the inside of a brain out to its surface. The brain is not finished. It is not close. Your job is to divide, again and again, and to make the cells of the cortex — the outer layer that will later handle thinking, memory and language.

Nobody hands you a blueprint. You get signals.

Here is the first one. You are burning sugar hard, because a dividing cell needs parts: new DNA, new membranes, new everything. Most of your sugar goes down one route, the pentose phosphate pathway, a chain of chemical steps that turns sugar into building material instead of plain energy. Now the sugar around you drops. Or something blocks that route.

You do not stop. You do not just make fewer cells. You make different ones: more inhibitory neurons, the quieting kind, plus cell types that normally belong to a later stage. Your calendar has moved.

The second signal is not chemistry. It is contact. A long fibre grows up towards you from the thalamus, a part deep in the brain that passes signals around the nervous system. In humans these fibres arrive early, long before they can connect to the neurons they will one day talk to. For years that early arrival looked like waiting.

It is not waiting. The fibre touches you. Where it touches, you make more excitatory neurons, the main signal-carriers of the cortex. The effect is strongest in the upper layers, the ones most expanded in humans. The team traces the touch to a gene called NRXN1, already known for helping neurons connect to each other, and already linked to autism. In models grown from patient cells carrying an NRXN1 mutation, the thalamic signals behaved differently, and the balance shifted between stem cells that stayed and neurons that got made.

You are a radial glia cell. Almost all of your kind will be gone before the baby is born. Aparna Bhaduri, whose UCLA lab worked on both studies, calls them "the coolest cells that have ever existed" — central to making us human, and central to disorders of brain development, mental illness and cancer. Cells that look like you turn up again in brain tumours decades later, and nobody fully knows why.

The old picture kept metabolism — the chemistry that turns food into parts — in the background, and put wiring last, once the parts existed. Both studies say no. Sugar and touch are instructions, and the cell reads them while it builds. That is how a mother's nutrition, a metabolic disorder, or a mutation in one connection gene could end up written into the shape of a cortex.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
Two papers from UCLA, one in Cell and one in Science. The Cell study mapped metabolism across the developing human cortex, using donated human tissue and brain organoids — small clumps of brain-like tissue grown from stem cells. Lowering glucose, the sugar cells run on, or blocking the pentose phosphate pathway changed what the stem cells produced.

The Science study used assembloids: organoids grown together so a thalamus-like piece and a cortex-like piece can meet. The thalamic fibres physically touched radial glia, and those cells then made more excitatory neurons. Some assembloids came from patient cells carrying an NRXN1 mutation.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
These are lab models, not living fetuses. Organoids and assembloids recreate important parts of human brain development, not all of it. The NRXN1 result is a shifted balance in a dish, not autism, and the gene is linked to the condition rather than shown here to cause it.

Nothing in this tells you how a particular diet in a real pregnancy would play out. And the tumour link stays open: radial-glia-like cells reappear in brain cancers for reasons scientists still do not understand.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Your cortex was not read off a plan. It was built from whatever the neighbourhood was saying at the time.

recall.q: When the sugar dropped, the stem cells did not make fewer neurons. What changed instead?
recall.a: Which neurons they made: more inhibitory ones, plus cell types that normally belong to a later stage. So sugar is not background fuel — it works as an instruction that steers the cell's decision.

cards.title: Do good people do better? Four possible answers
cards.body: Ask whether the world rewards good people and you are really asking about the shape of a curve. It could rise, fall, stay flat — or peak in the middle, with saints and monsters both punished. And even a rising curve would not prove the world is just.

sections.text:
Eric Schwitzgebel has a recipe for settling the oldest question about fairness. Take out your moralometer and your happiness-meter. Test a random sample of everyone who has ever lived, plot one score against the other, and read the shape of the curve.

The meters are the joke. The shape is not. There are only so many shapes it could be, and each one needs something different to be true.

1. Moral order. The better you act, the better your life goes, all the way up the scale. This needs something doing the work, and there are two familiar answers. Inside the person: guilt eats at you, a secret wrong keeps everyone at a distance, one crime pulls you into the next until it all falls apart — Macbeth, Crime and Punishment. Outside the person: treat people well and they treat you well, criminals are usually caught, and society notices who behaves well.

2. Moral disorder. There is no link at all. The good and the wicked are equally likely to thrive or suffer. This one needs nothing to work. It is what you see if those forces are real but too weak to bend the line.

3. Immoral order. The wicked tend to thrive and the good tend to suffer. This needs goodness to cost something real, and often it does. Let the others off the sinking boat first and you are likelier to drown. Give your money away and you have nothing in reserve when illness or job loss arrives. The most successful politicians, business leaders and film stars are not, Schwitzgebel notes, "a parade of saints".

4. Mediocrity thrives. Both ends do badly and the middle does best. This needs other people to punish the extremes, and they may. Very good people are often disliked: they make everyone else look bad. Groups reward fitting in, and standing far from the people around you is uncomfortable in either direction.

Two problems cut across all four. The first: the answer depends on which morality you measure. If being good means giving away nearly everything you own to the world's poorest, goodness is expensive and the curve sags. A gentler morality — one that values close relationships and allows some comfort — fits an ordered world far more easily. The ancient Chinese philosopher Mengzi went furthest: what pleases the heart is good, and what is good pleases the heart. Then goodness and happiness travel together by design.

Schwitzgebel's own guess assumes that gentler morality. In most well-running societies, he thinks, there is a real link between acting well and living well: positive, imperfect, small to medium in size.

The second problem is sharper. Even a rising curve may not mean what it looks like. People who are already comfortable can more easily afford to be generous, patient and forgiving. Unhappiness can push people into behaving badly. If the arrow runs that way, the world is ordered — but it is not paying anyone back for being good.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: An ordered world and a just world are not the same world.

recall.q: Even if good people really do tend to do better, why might that still not show a just world?
recall.a: Because the cause could run the other way. People who are already comfortable can more easily afford to be generous and forgiving, and unhappiness can push people into behaving badly. The curve would rise without anyone being repaid for being good.

cards.title: A Linux backdoor that never touches the source code
cards.body: Read every line of a program's source code and find nothing wrong. Build it. The program that comes out has a backdoor. Five researchers say they did this to an entire Linux distribution — the whole operating system, not one program — without changing a line of source.
cards.evidence: single preprint · v1, 27 Jul 2026 · not peer reviewed

sections.text:
A compiler is the tool that turns source code into a binary — the file a machine actually runs. Poison that binary and it does two jobs. It hides a backdoor in the programs it builds. It also hides the same poison in the next compiler it builds.

So clean source keeps producing a dirty compiler. Reading the code does not help: the code is honest. Rebuilding does not help: the thing doing the building is the thing that lies. The paper calls this the trusting-trust attack.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Preprint posted to arXiv on 27 July 2026, version 1, not peer reviewed
Five authors, first listed: Julien Malka
Filed under cs.CR (security) and cs.SE (software engineering)

sections.label: What it showed, what it didn't
sections.text: It shows the attack can be built, because the authors built it. It does not name the distribution, the scale, or whether any check that distribution already runs caught the tampering. And it is no evidence that anyone has shipped a poisoned system to real users.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Almost all trust in open-source software rests on one idea: anyone can read the source. This attack sits underneath that layer. One poisoned compiler, every program on the machine.

recall.q: The source code is clean, and rebuilding from that clean source does not fix the problem. Why not?
recall.a: The lie lives in the compiler binary, not in the code. The compiler puts a backdoor into the programs it builds, and puts the same poison into the next compiler it builds — so honest source keeps producing a poisoned tool.

cards.title: Monitoring workers doesn't raise output. It raises stress.
cards.body: Companies are on track to spend more than $4 billion in 2026 watching employees, keystroke by keystroke. A pooled analysis of more than 23,000 workers found no link between how closely people were watched and how well they worked. What did move output was what workers were told about why.
cards.evidence: research review · pooled analysis of 23,000+ subjects (2022) · survey of 3,500+ Canadian workers (2024) · lab and workpl

sections.text:
A US postal worker gets asked why they scanned a package twice. The answer exists, because everything does. Every scan carries a time. Every stop carries a location. The GPS marker moves with the van, live, on somebody else's screen. Writing on Reddit in 2025, one carrier said the job now feels less like public service and more like "a quiet surveillance state."

That hour is ordinary now. A 2022 New York Times investigation found that eight of the ten largest private employers in the US tracked how much individual workers produced, often in real time — UPS, Amazon and UnitedHealth among them. Michele Molè, who studies employment law at the University of Groningen, says adding a monitoring app to a workplace is now about as easy as downloading Spotify. So the plain question is whether it works.

Mostly it does not. Cornelius König, a psychology researcher at Saarland University in Germany, reviewed the evidence in 2025 and found little sign that electronic monitoring lifts performance. Daniel Ravid at the University of New Mexico ran a meta-analysis in 2022 — a study that pools the results of many earlier studies — covering more than 23,000 people across labs, call centers, offices and police patrols. Across all of it, how closely people were watched had no link to how well they worked.

Two human habits explain why. The first: people get used to being watched. Effort lifts for a while, then settles back. König points to police body cameras, as public and high-stakes as watching gets, which over the long run do not much change how officers or the public behave. The second: people push back to feel free again. Ravid describes the worker who taps a key every so often while reading a book through lunch.

The costs do not fade. Ravid found that monitoring of any kind — light or heavy, open or hidden — raised stress at work. A 2024 survey of more than 3,500 Canadian workers matched that: those who believed they were being watched reported more pressure, and less privacy and control. Measurement can also bend behavior in strange directions. In a 2020 study, electronically monitored truck drivers broke the daily driving-hour limits less often, and crashed more.

The most useful finding is about trust, not tools. In a 2024 trial, strong remote workers were allowed to switch their monitoring software off. Whether their output held depended entirely on what they were told when the offer arrived. The researchers concluded that money spent on good managers beats money spent on software. Ravid's data points the same way: workers who know exactly what is collected, and why, report more fairness and more job satisfaction than workers watched without explanation.

Which leaves the marker on the screen. König says many companies collect the data because the tools exist, not because any plan needs it, and end up with terabytes sitting on a drive nobody opens. Kirstie Ball of the University of St Andrews asks the question they skip: are you measuring what you think you are measuring, or looking because you can? The van keeps moving. Most of what it records will never be read by anyone.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: A 2024 study followed remote workers on Upwork, a site where companies hire freelancers. Top performers were offered the chance to turn the monitoring software off. When the offer came with no explanation, their output fell by nearly 20 percent. When the same group was told the freedom was theirs because their results had been impressive, output held. The software was not holding the work up. The reason was.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: These are averages, not a verdict on every workplace. Monitoring clearly helps somewhere: an Australian mining company used headbands that read brainwaves and cut fatigue-related accidents to almost zero. The Canadian survey measured what workers felt, not what the systems actually did. And no overall link still leaves room for one tool, in one job, to work.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: You can measure someone all day and still never give them a reason to try.

recall.q: Strong remote workers were offered the chance to switch their monitoring software off. What decided whether their output dropped?
recall.a: The explanation. With no reason given, output fell by nearly 20 percent. Told the freedom was earned by their strong results, output held. The trust the offer signaled, not the software, was doing the work.

cards.title: AI and the Crow: when a value stops making sense
cards.body: Young Crow on the reservation still said counting coups. But the acts it counted had been outlawed, so the phrase pointed at nothing. Jonathan Lear calls this a rare human fate: your values do not become wrong, or old-fashioned. They become unintelligible — there is nothing left for them to be about. One essay argues that merit is now open in exactly that way.

sections.text:
Touch an enemy fighter with your stick: that counts. Untie a horse inside his camp and lead it home: that counts too. The Crow called this counting coups. The tally was how a man's worth was read.

In 1884 the United States moved the Crow onto a reservation. Tribal war was outlawed. Taking a horse from another camp became a matter for the local police. Young Crow still said counting coups. There was nothing left to count.

Plenty Coups, the last Crow chief, told his life story to a white writer, Frank Linderman. Linderman added a note at the end. He could not get the old chief to speak about anything after the buffalo were killed off. "After this nothing happened."

Things did happen. He married, moved onto the reservation, testified before Congress for his people. He still called those years empty. The philosopher Jonathan Lear, in his book Radical Hope, thinks he meant it exactly. The Crow's values had not become old-fashioned, or wrong, or worth arguing over. They had become unintelligible. There was nothing left for them to be about.

This, the essay's authors say, is the AI risk almost nobody names. The usual worries are material: jobs, water, electricity, inequality. All real. But they skip what should frighten anyone who writes or teaches. The concepts we argue with are being hollowed out.

Take merit. It is our tally: how we decide what deserves praise, money, attention, blame. We fight about it constantly, and the fighting proves the idea is alive. Large language models — the programs behind chatbots — do not join that fight. They show how easily a machine's work can pass as your own. Cheating is the narrow edge of this, and teachers already feel it. The wider version has no name. If a machine will do any task, doing the work yourself becomes like using a typewriter today: a hobby, not a standard anyone can be held to.

Authenticity, expertise and deliberation sit in the same place, pressed by one idea: all that matters about an output is whether it works — code, a college essay, a love letter. What is left of romantic love if we cannot say why it matters that the note was written by the person sending it? How do you hold a child to standards of effort you no longer keep? Pretty Shield, a Crow medicine woman, told Linderman what raising children on the reservation felt like: "I am trying to live a life that I do not understand."

Plenty Coups could not stop any of it. He worked with the whites and spared his people the worse fates other tribes met. But what Lear calls his radical hope was not about making reservation life comfortable. It was his ability to imagine a future in which the Crow could again live a life clearly their own. The essay wants something smaller and more urgent: not hope for a return, but keeping our concepts alive now. Hence its plain list. Reading groups in the Catskills with no devices. Campus rules that make a classroom closer to a religious order. Not museums for dead ideas. Training grounds.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: How far does the case stretch? Not all the way, and the essay admits it. The Crow had one shared set of practices; we are plural and divided. Nobody is destroying our food supply either. These are products we choose, and many people say the tools have made their work better and their thinking sharper. The authors say to listen to them. But their darkest point cuts against their own comfort. The Crow's ending can at least be told from outside, as the price of progress. If what is traded away is human judgement itself — some founders speak of people as a resource to use up, and welcome the merge of man and machine — nobody is left outside to tell it that way.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The word can outlive the thing it named. That is why the loss is so easy to miss.

recall.q: Young Crow on the reservation still said counting coups. Why did Lear not find that reassuring?
recall.a: The word survived, but the acts it counted had been outlawed, so it pointed at nothing real. That is his point: a value can die not by being rejected, but by becoming unintelligible. The essay argues merit could go the same way, with the word still in daily use.

cards.title: They still lost focus. They just stopped daydreaming.
cards.body: Nine people with damage to one small patch at the front of the brain almost never reported inner thoughts during a dull task — no memories, no plans. But noises in the room still pulled them away, and so did the dull task itself, as often as they did for everyone else. That split says mind-wandering does not start with losing focus. It starts with something building a scene for you to wander into.
cards.evidence: single study · n=42 (9 patients with vmPFC damage) · lesion study · self-report probes

sections.text:
Every forty trials or so, the screen stopped and asked where your attention had just been.

The task in between was built to be dull. Horizontal lines, over and over; press the button when a vertical set appears. If you said your attention had drifted, you had to say what kind of drift: an inner thought, a thought about the task, or something outside you, like a noise in the room. If it was inner, you also said whether it pointed to the past, the present, or the future.

That sorting is the whole point. Psychologists use the word mind-wandering for thought that breaks away from what is in front of you and runs on its own material — a memory, a plan. Brain scans have long tied it to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, a small area low in the front of the brain. Damage there was already known to reduce mind-wandering. Nobody knew why.

Two explanations fit. Either that region builds the wandering thoughts, or it only lets you notice that you have wandered. The two predict different mistakes. If the region does the noticing, patients should report less of every kind of drift, inner and outer alike. If it builds the thoughts, one column should empty and the rest should stay full.

One column emptied. Elisa Ciaramelli's team in Bologna tested nine patients whose damage was limited to that region. They reported far fewer inner thoughts than either comparison group, and what went missing was the past and the future. Their task-related thoughts and their outside distractions ran at normal levels. They could still lose focus. They simply had nothing waiting inside to lose focus into.

Then the researchers handed them the material. Cue words appeared under the centre of the screen — seaside, and others like it — chosen to pull up personal memories. The patients still produced fewer inner thoughts from those cues than healthy adults did. Again, the shortfall sat only in the inner column.

So the claim is narrow and solid. This region is needed to build inner scenes on your own, and mind-wandering starts with that building, not with a failure to stay on task. What the study cannot say is what the loss costs. Does a mind that never wanders plan worse, reflect less, or solve problems less creatively? This work raises that question and leaves it open.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: 42 people in all: nine patients with damage limited to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, 14 patients with brain damage in other areas, and 19 healthy adults. Everyone did two versions of the same line task — one plain, one with cue words under the centre point of the screen.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Nine patients is a small number, and the researchers say so: the test is not sensitive enough to catch small differences between the two patient groups, so a real one could hide there unseen. The method also asks people to label their own thoughts on demand. Nobody watched these patients catch themselves daydreaming without a prompt, so this result holds for one way of asking.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Losing focus and wandering are not the same act. The second one needs something built for you to wander into.

recall.q: The patients lost focus as often as everyone else, but reported almost no inner thoughts. Why does that split answer the question the researchers were asking?
recall.a: If the damaged region only helped you notice that you had drifted, every kind of drift would have been under-reported. Instead only inner thoughts dropped, while thoughts about the task and outside distractions stayed normal. So the region builds the inner content rather than watching for it.

cards.title: China's GLM-5.3 beat Anthropic on one hacking test
cards.body: A Chinese open-source model beat Anthropic's best released model at finding software security flaws, 84.5% to 83.8%. At turning those flaws into working attacks, it lost badly: 54.4% to 78.0%. And the American model in that test finished training back in January. It was held back on purpose.

sections.text:
The US debate on AI rarely mentions China. Four numbers from the hacking benchmarks.

1. China won a headline test, barely. Z.ai's open-source GLM-5.3 scored 84.5% on CyberGym, which asks a model to read code, find security flaws, and confirm they are real. Anthropic's Mythos 5 got 83.8%.

2. On the harder step, the gap is wide. ExploitBench measures turning a flaw into a working attack: 54.4% for GLM-5.3, 78.0% for Mythos 5. On the clock, GLM-5.3 built 105 attacks in two hours and 130 in six. Mythos built 181 and 247.

3. Mythos is not America's best model, only the best released one. Mythos Preview came out in April, four months before GLM-5.3. The original finished training in January and was held back over cybersecurity worries. A fast follower has fewer of those.

4. Where this is weakest: Z.ai reported every one of these numbers itself, and no outsider has checked them. Anthropic's stronger unreleased models are also just Anthropic's word. The lead is real. Its size is not measured.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: AI hacking has no mutually assured destruction — no promise that the attacker suffers too. A country with a big, lasting model lead could empty the other's bank and brokerage accounts, and the victim could not hack back: its weaker model would be busy defending. So the size of the gap matters more than who is ahead on paper.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: This lead is policy as much as technology. The one named way to lose it: pushing Chinese AI talent out of the United States.

recall.q: GLM-5.3's 84.5% looks like a near-tie. What two things in the piece make America's lead bigger than that number suggests?
recall.a: GLM-5.3 only won at spotting flaws. At building working attacks it scored 54.4% against Mythos 5's 78.0%, and finished 105 attacks in two hours against Mythos's 181. And Mythos is not America's best model, only the best released one — trained back in January and delayed over cybersecurity worries.

cards.title: Mars kept the record of early life that Earth buried
cards.body: A paper in Nature describes small spots in a Mars rock. They match the mineral leftovers of long-dead microbes. Erik Hoel's point is stranger than the finding. Earth buries and paves over the evidence of its own beginning. Mars — no moving crust, nobody walking on it — kept its record untouched. If these exact marks turned up on Earth, he says, they would go straight into the textbooks on early life.
cards.evidence: single Nature paper · one rock target at Cheyava Falls · measured by instruments on Mars, limits acknowledged

sections.text:
An arrow-shaped rock, only a few feet across, sits at the bottom of a river that dried up long ago. The river is on Mars. Neuroscientist and philosopher Erik Hoel wants you to follow one line through this rock's story. It runs backwards from what you would expect. The living planet loses the record of how life began. The dead one keeps it.

Start on Earth. Some of the oldest chemical evidence for life here is not a fossil. It is minerals left by microbes that ran on iron and sulfur — they pulled energy from those elements the way we pull it from oxygen and sugar. Before life had bones or shells to leave behind, marks in rock are all there is.

Then Earth went to work on itself. Plate tectonics is the slow movement of the crust: old sea floor slides under and is destroyed. It buried much of that early record. What the crust missed, we covered — foundations, roads, footsteps. The planet where life began is the planet least able to show you the beginning.

Mars has none of that. No plates to pull the old rock down, nobody building on top of it. That is Hoel's museum: not a place that protects its exhibits, but a place where nothing ever came to disturb them.

On Wednesday, mostly lost in the week's news, a paper in Nature described what NASA found in that rock, at a spot called Cheyava Falls. The rock is red with iron oxide — rust. Inside the red sit small bleached spots, nicknamed leopard spots. Microbes that run on iron and sulfur leave patterns like these. On Earth the same shapes turn up in sea-floor mud and in very old rock, where they have their own names: reduction halos and reduction spots.

Hoel's sharpest move is a thought experiment. Move this exact evidence to Earth. Scientists would call it biological and move on. A non-living explanation would be taken less seriously, and the finding would land in textbooks about early life. On Mars we call it a biosignature — a pattern that fits life without proving it. It is the same kind of evidence we already accept about our own past before fossils. Arguably better evidence, Hoel says, once you allow for the limits of instruments sitting on another planet.

Notice how quietly it arrived. Other claims of alien life get loud — shaky signals from planets light-years away, or the swinging excitement around a comet from outside our solar system. Here the scientists were careful with their words and careful with their method. The story sank under the week's noise.

So the argument points one way: go. Not only as science. Hoel is blunt that people often act like low creatures — vultures over the dead, snakes that strike and slide away. He does not believe that is what we are. He thinks we need something to remind us, and a small arrow-shaped rock in a dry riverbed did that for him.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Nobody in the paper says life. The careful words are possible indications, and biosignature rather than fossil. Non-living chemistry can make spots like these too, and that dull explanation has to be cleared first. What the paper can say is that there is currently no evidence this particular rock went through those processes. No evidence found is not the same as ruled out. Which is exactly why Hoel's answer is go and look, not case closed.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Earth buried the story of its own beginning. Mars left it lying in a dry riverbed.

recall.q: Hoel says these same spots, found on Earth, would be called biological without much argument. So why does he think the dead planet holds the better record?
recall.a: Because Earth destroys its own early record. Plate tectonics drags old crust down and buries it, and where the crust missed, people built on top. Mars has no moving plates and nobody building, so the rock at Cheyava Falls has sat undisturbed.

cards.title: Your watch measures steps. It guesses deep sleep.
cards.body: A smartwatch has good sensors. But not every number on the screen is a measurement. Some are guesses dressed up as facts — and one simple rule tells you which is which.
cards.evidence: framework paper · University of Michigan kinesiologists · no accuracy figures reported

sections.text:
Two numbers on the same screen this morning: resting heart rate 58, deep sleep 58 minutes. Same font, same size, same confident look. Guess before you read on — would a hospital lab agree with both, one, or neither?

Most people say both. The watch sat on your wrist all night and never asked you a single question. Others say neither, because it is a gadget and gadgets exaggerate. The answer is one. Kinesiologists at the University of Michigan — scientists who study how the body moves — recently published a framework for reading these devices, and it splits the screen in half.

Under the case sit four sensors: an accelerometer for movement, a gyroscope for turning, GPS for location, and a photoplethysmogram, or PPG — a small light that shines into your skin and reads changes in blood volume. The raw data they collect is good. The trouble starts after that. Everything you read has passed through the company's private software, which turns a signal into a number.

Their rule is simple. The farther a number sits from the raw sensor data, the less you should trust it. Heart rate, step count and outdoor pace stay close to the signal and hold up well. Calories burned, sleep stages, blood glucose and water lost during exercise sit far from it. So the 58 beats is the solid number. The 58 minutes is a guess built on a guess.

Why does this surprise us? The screen gives no clue. A measured number and a guessed one are printed to the same minute, in the same font, with no margin of error and no hint of doubt. "People shouldn't take these metrics at face value," said Adam Lepley, one of the authors; the devices suit tracking trends over time better than precise measurement. That is the part worth keeping. If your deep sleep number falls steadily for two weeks, that pattern means something. The 58 on its own does not.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Trust the count, not the score. Steps and heart rate sit near the sensor. Recovery time and readiness ratings sit at the far end — the researchers say to take those with a grain of salt.
Switch brands and your sleep and calorie numbers change overnight, while nothing about you changed. Different private algorithms, different answers.
Compare yourself only to yourself: same watch, same wrist, across weeks. That is the only comparison these numbers can carry.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is a framework — a way of sorting what is measured from what is guessed. No error figures here. It tells you which numbers sit further from the sensor, not how far off any single reading is.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A number printed to the minute is not the same as a number that was measured.

recall.q: Your watch shows a resting heart rate and a deep-sleep total in the same font. What decides which one you can trust?
recall.a: How far the number sits from the raw sensor data. Heart rate, step count and outdoor pace stay close to what the sensors pick up, so they hold up. Sleep stages, calories, hydration and glucose are built by private software several steps away — useful as trends, not as measurements.

cards.title: 3M knew in the 1970s: forever chemicals in our blood
cards.body: In the 1970s a 3M scientist found the company's chemicals in the blood of ordinary people who had never worked there. Lawyers told him to keep it to himself. Twenty years later a young 3M chemist found the same thing — and was told, again and again, that she must have made a mistake.

sections.text:
1970s. A 3M scientist finds PFOS — a forever chemical, one that does not break down in the body — in the blood of people who never worked for 3M. The company's lawyers tell him to say nothing.

1996. Chemist Kris Hansen joins 3M's environmental lab. An outside lab is comparing worker blood with clean samples from a blood bank, and something odd keeps showing up in the clean ones. Find the contaminant, she is told.

Late 1990s. It is not a contaminant. PFOS is in blood-bank samples, in a colleague's horses, in fish, in eagles. Colleagues insist she made a mistake. Only archived blood from Korean War recruits, drawn in the early 1950s, comes back clean — so the rest is real, and 3M is the source. A senior colleague then mentions the 1970s finding. She is the second person to find it.

Early 1999. She presents to the CEO, who falls asleep. She is taken off PFOS work.

Late 1990s to 2002. 3M tells the EPA it has found PFOS in blood across the country, while stating there are "no adverse effects". Under EPA pressure it stops making PFOS in 2002 — and switches to another forever chemical that also builds up in the body.

2021. A former professor sends Hansen a John Oliver segment on the health harms of PFAS, the wider family PFOS belongs to. Her first thought is that it is wrong.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Early 1950s — blood drawn from Korean War recruits, the only samples that came back clean
About 20 years — the gap between the first finding and the second
2002 — 3M stops making PFOS under EPA pressure; a replacement forever chemical takes its place
More than 100 — cattle dead downstream of a DuPont site in West Virginia, the case behind the film Dark Waters

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: No records were burned. On this account the secret held because one junior scientist was doubted so steadily — clean your equipment, who told you to do this, why are you doing this — that she stopped raising it. It held because she was told the chemicals were safe, and she wanted that to be true. Polluted ground can be cleaned up. PFAS are now reported in every country and in nearly every body. Blood cannot be cleaned up.

recall.q: The 1970s finding and Hansen's finding were the same. What kept the gap between them open for about twenty years?
recall.a: The first finding was buried on legal advice, so almost nobody knew it existed. When Hansen found it again, colleagues and executives treated her data as an error rather than a result, while assuring her the chemicals were safe. Steady doubt plus false comfort was enough — no records had to be destroyed.

cards.title: Psilocybin never reaches your brain. Psilocin does.
cards.body: The drug everyone names is not the one that acts. Psilocybin is a prodrug: the gut and liver cut a piece off it to make psilocin, and psilocin is what enters the brain. The first trial to give humans psilocin directly since the 1960s found the experience almost identical — with somewhat fewer bad side effects.
cards.evidence: single study · n=20, 18 per condition · crossover, healthy experienced volunteers · no placebo arm, no blood levels meas

sections.text:
The capsule holds 25 milligrams of psilocybin. By the time anything reaches the brain, none of it is left.

Almost everyone treats psilocybin as the drug: the headlines, the people taking it. Fair guess. It is the name on the bottle, and nearly every modern trial has used the same thing — 25 mg of synthetic psilocybin in a capsule.

But psilocybin does not make the psychedelic effect. It is a prodrug, meaning the body must break it apart before it does anything at all. Swallow it, and enzymes in the gut and liver cut off a small part called a phosphate. What is left is psilocin, and psilocin is what crosses into the brain and changes what you see and feel. A 2019 study found that how strong a trip feels tracks how much psilocin is moving in the blood.

That extra step is not free. People convert at different rates. That is one likely reason a fixed 25 mg dose lands so differently in different bodies.

So why not skip the step and give psilocin itself? Nobody had given it to a human since the 1960s. Josh Woolley's team at the University of California, San Francisco did.

They expected psilocin to arrive faster. It did not. Start, peak, length — the two capsules were nearly the same, and both brought deep psychological insight and mystical-type experiences.

The difference showed up in what went wrong. Nearly everyone had mild problems on both, but psilocybin was linked to more moderate and severe ones: headaches, anxiety, one brief loss of consciousness. Nausea was equally common on both, so an upset stomach is not simply the price of breaking psilocybin down. Woolley calls the gap "modest, not dramatic" — fewer and milder events on average, across 18 people per condition. A signal, not a settled finding.

The third arm was psilocin held under the tongue, which skips the gut entirely. It was safe and easy to tolerate, but much weaker: lower intensity ratings, smaller changes in heart rate and blood pressure. Little of the drug reached the blood at doses this cautious. The route was never really put to the test.

And yet those tiny doses under the tongue produced emotional-breakthrough scores in the range of the full 25 mg. Woolley is careful about it: it could be noise, or the therapy in the room rather than the drug. If it holds, it puts a question under the whole model — whether the overwhelming experience is the part doing the work.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
Twenty healthy adults, aged 25 to 50. All had used psychedelics before, and all reported mild social disconnection. Each person came back for up to four sessions, four weeks apart, so every comparison happens inside the same body.

Three treatments: a psilocybin capsule (25 mg), a psilocin capsule (17.5 mg, chosen to match it), and a psilocin tablet under the tongue — starting at 2.18 mg, later raised to 4.36 mg or 8 mg. Sessions ran in a clinic room with eyeshades and music, a therapist and an assistant present throughout. Heart rate and blood pressure were tracked. Participants rated the drug's strength every 15 to 30 minutes. All three products were standardised whole-mushroom extracts, not lab-made chemicals.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
Twenty people, all healthy, highly educated, already used to psychedelics — not the patients these drugs are meant to treat. There was no inactive placebo. And because the under-the-tongue tablets felt so much milder, participants and therapists could often guess what they had been given, which can bend self-reported scores.

No blood was drawn during sessions, so nobody knows how much psilocin actually reached the blood; Woolley names this the main limitation. The whole-mushroom-versus-synthetic comparison used data from an earlier trial with different people, so it shows no big difference rather than ruling one out. All of this happened with pharmaceutical-grade product under constant medical supervision — the loss of consciousness was handled because clinicians were in the room. "A first look, not a verdict."

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The name on the capsule is not the molecule your brain meets.

recall.q: Psilocybin has to change before it can act. What does the body turn it into, and what happened when the trial gave people that molecule directly?
recall.a: The gut and liver cut a phosphate off psilocybin to make psilocin, and psilocin is what enters the brain. Giving psilocin directly skipped that step, but the start, peak and length of the experience were nearly the same as psilocybin. The main difference was somewhat fewer moderate and severe side effects.

cards.title: Ingeborg Bachmann: a 1971 novel and 580 pages of letters
cards.body: Malina (1971) opens with a woman, the man she lives with, and the married man up the same street. In life, Ingeborg Bachmann's lover was Max Frisch, the leading Swiss novelist of his time. Their letters run about 580 pages, under the title "We did not do it well." Read together, the letters and the novel keep touching.

sections.text:
A woman lives with one man. She loves another. That one is married, has more charm, and lives right up the same street.

That is how Malina opens — an Austrian novel from 1971 by Ingeborg Bachmann. A reader on the blog Marginal Revolution is going through it in German. They call that setup only the start; the book does not stay there. Their verdict is blunt: stunned by how good it is, and deeper than any of the famous nineteenth-century novels by women.

One warning comes attached. In English, it seems less good.

Bachmann is being read again anyway. A new biography arrived this year, by Dieter Burdorf, called Dieses unruhige Ich — this restless I. Ich is simply the German word for I, the self.

The restlessness left a paper trail. For years her lover was Max Frisch. Their letters have been published in German at roughly 580 pages, titled Wir haben es nicht gut gemacht — we did not do it well. Frisch wrote his side elsewhere too: his book Montauk is partly about the two of them.

The striking thing in the letters is not the damage. It is the persistence — how many ups and downs one relationship can take and still continue. Four hundred pages in, with about 180 to go, the reader is not bored.

Their advice: take a few letters at a time. Read fast and the whole story rushes past. Read slow and it keeps the size of a life. Somewhere in there the letters begin touching Malina — the same material handled twice, once lived, once made into a novel.

The friction for us is not her era. It is the language. Almost all of this sits in German: the letters, the poems, the biography just published. In German-speaking Europe she is hardly a secret. There is a film of Malina, an opera, and a biopic about her and Frisch.

That is loosening. The Frisch letters come out in English in November, and letters may cross over better than novels do. A new edition of her short stories arrives in English this fall. The order is odd: the side material travels first, while the novel that started all of it loses the most in the crossing.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one reader's enthusiasm, caught early and out loud. They are four hundred pages into the letters, have only started the biography, and have not read the Celan letters. Ranking Malina above the nineteenth-century novels is taste, not a verdict. And the report that it thins out in English comes from someone who reads German — which most of us cannot check.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Discovery gets rarer the more you know. That is exactly why, when someone new turns up, you follow them.

recall.q: The Bachmann–Frisch letters are titled "We did not do it well." What does the reader working through them find remarkable — and why only a few at a time?
recall.a: Not the failure, but the persistence: how many ups and downs one relationship can take and still keep going. A few letters at a time keeps that slow shape, instead of letting a life rush past as a plot.

cards.title: Nature helps a stressed mind. A calm one? Barely studied.
cards.body: Forty years of research show that parks and forests repair a tired, stressed mind. A Berlin team asked the other half of the question — what nature does for someone already well. They found eight studies, against 45 on recovery. The gap is not laziness. People walk in the park exactly when they feel the need, so repair and buildup are almost impossible to tell apart.
cards.evidence: literature review · 8 studies on healthy people vs 45 on stressed people · different tests, effect sizes not comparable

sections.text:
A team of neuroscientists in Berlin, led by Simone Kühn at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, found that gap sitting in the middle of a forty-year-old field. Here is where things stand, easiest question first.

Why does anyone think nature helps?

One study, 1984, in the journal Science. Roger Ulrich followed patients recovering from gall bladder surgery. The ones whose window faced a garden instead of a brick wall healed a day faster, needed less pain medicine, and had fewer problems after the operation. That same year E.O. Wilson published Biophilia, which argued that humans have an inborn pull toward living things. A field grew out of the two of them.

How much nature do you need?

Less than you would think. Ten minutes in a park or a forest is enough to show benefits. Even looking at a picture of nature helps a little — co-author Johanna Prugger changed her phone background to a forest because of it. The effect is uneven: the more worn out you are, the more easily the benefit arrives.

Does it do anything if you are already well?

This is the question almost nobody asked. Only eight studies in the review compared nature with a city street for people who were not stressed or ill. Those eight found gains in thinking, and mostly good effects on mood and emotion. But each used a different test, so their results cannot be lined up against each other.

What even counts as nature?

Not only wild places. Neat, trimmed gardens still work. An Italian group compared modern streets full of traffic with old quarters — churches, cobblestones, people on foot — and the old quarters came out more restful. So nature works like a slider, not a switch, and rounded shapes rest the attention better than sharp edges. Real wilderness may run the other way: a path where you could fall off a cliff carries a threat, and threat is not restful.

And the one nobody can answer yet. Does nature build a shield in advance — protection against stress that has not happened? The Berlin team thinks that kind of strength grows slowly, with repetition. Ordinary walks cannot test it. People go to the park exactly when they feel the need, which turns every result back into recovery. A real test would need walks at fixed hours, set before the mood arrives.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is a review of other people's work, not a new experiment, and only eight studies met the narrow bar of comparing nature with a city. Nearly all of it comes from Europe, the US and Canada, where the nature studied is the same kind of managed park or forest — do not stretch the findings to the whole world. You always know whether you are in a park, so nobody can be kept blind to their group, and a placebo effect cannot be ruled out. Prugger's only answer: the effects first showed up forty years ago, before nature became a media topic. A recent attempt to repeat Ulrich's 1991 nature-video study half worked — the mind effects held up, the body effects came out mixed.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Forty years of evidence that nature repairs a person. Almost none that it builds one.

recall.q: Why is it so hard to test whether nature strengthens a healthy person instead of repairing a tired one?
recall.a: Because people go to the park exactly when they already feel the need, so any gain reads as recovery. Telling the two apart would need walks at fixed hours, set before the mood arrives.

cards.title: Rumi asks: why adore the dead but battle the living?
cards.body: An eight-hundred-year-old poem catches a habit we still have: we give the dead a tenderness we refuse the living. Read closely, Rumi does more than complain. He shows that the love you are not giving tonight is not missing. It is being held back.

sections.text:
Someone kneels at a grave and presses their mouth to cold stone. The person under that stone had a face for years. It was right there, warm, and nobody kissed it.

Rumi wrote about that gap. He lived from 1207 to 1273 — sixty-six years, and nearly sixty-six thousand verses. Three lines from one short poem, in Haleh Liza Gafori's new English version:

"Let's love each other, let's cherish each other, my friend, before we lose each other."

"So why put me on trial while I'm alive? Why adore the dead but battle the living?"

"You'll kiss the headstone of my grave... Kiss my face instead!"

Now go slowly, clause by clause.

"Let's" is an offer, not an order. And he speaks to a friend — not a lover, not a dying parent. This is aimed at the people you see on normal days.

"Before we lose each other" is the deadline. Notice it is not "before I die." The loss runs both ways, and it has no date. Rumi puts an appointment in your calendar and will not say when. A deadline like that is easy to ignore. He opens with it anyway.

Then the poem turns to the future, and it sounds sure. You will miss him. You will settle the quarrel — later, once he is gone. Not "you might." It tells you what you are going to do. Naming it early makes today look like a choice, not a mood.

"Put me on trial" is a courtroom word, and that is the whole move. Nobody feels like a prosecutor — the person who builds the case against you. You feel busy, or fair, or tired, or simply right. The word says a case is already open, and you are the one running it.

The next question puts the two habits side by side — adore the dead, battle the living — and asks what rule joins them. There is no rule. Any honest answer makes you the problem. And notice what the line does not do. It never calls the graveside love fake. It accepts it fully. The feeling is real. Only its aim is wrong.

Then the speaker lies down. He plays dead inside his own poem, still as stone, so you can watch yourself kiss the headstone while he is still alive to see it. The last line holds the poem's only exclamation mark. Its heaviest word is the smallest one: instead. Not "as well." The kiss is not missing. You have it. You are pointing it at rock.

So this is not a poem about grief. It is a poem about supply. If the tenderness you will spend at the grave exists, it exists tonight, and something is holding it. Not-loving is not an empty space waiting for love to arrive. It is an act. It has a hand on it, and an author.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: Are these Rumi's exact words? No. Gafori says plainly that English cannot carry the Persian sound — the inner rhymes, the wordplay, the music that drives the original. Persian poetry also leans on grand, abstract phrasing that modern English avoids, so she wrote for an English ear. What crosses over is the structure: the dateless deadline, the courtroom word, the small "instead." That is what a close reading like this can honestly claim.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Nobody discovers new love at a graveside. They spend what they were already holding.

recall.q: Rumi never says the love people pour out at a graveside is fake. Why does accepting it make his point sharper, not softer?
recall.a: Because if that love is real at the grave, it was already there while the person was alive. So today's coldness is not an empty space waiting to be filled. It is love being held back and aimed somewhere else. That is the work his word "instead" does: you have the kiss, you are just pointing it at stone.

cards.title: India let the rupee float for 883 days. It swung 7.4%.
cards.body: From June 2009 to October 2011 the RBI almost stopped trading in the currency market. It is the one real stretch of a free-floating rupee in modern India. The rupee swung 7.4 percent a year, against 4.98 percent today. Three economists now read that window as the price tag on a hands-off rupee.

sections.text:
The RBI buys and sells dollars most months to hold the rupee steady. For 883 days it nearly stopped. Its monthly trading stayed under 1 percent of M0 — the base money the RBI itself creates. Rounak Hande, Rajeswari Sengupta and Ajay Shah treat that gap as a natural experiment: the closest India has come to a rupee set purely by the market.

The rupee also stopped being a dollar-only story. In the float, the euro and the yen moved it too. Under the peg, and again today, only the dollar shows up.

sections.label: The numbers
items: The float: 1 June 2009 to 31 October 2011 — 28 months, 883 days.
Rupee-dollar swing: 7.40% floating, 1.43% under the 2023–24 peg, 4.98% now.
Pull of a 1% dollar move on the rupee: 0.66% floating, 0.89% pegged, 0.79% now.
Daily rupee trading, onshore and offshore: about $40bn then, about $140bn now.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The RBI's whole currency operation buys about 2.4 percentage points of calm — 7.4 down to 4.98. And 7.4 probably overstates what a float would cost today. In 2009–11 the rupee had no anchor; now the RBI targets 4 percent inflation. The market is also three times deeper, and a deeper market is a steadier one.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: One puzzle stays open. Today the rupee follows a falling dollar at 0.88 but a rising one at only 0.68. That looks like the RBI leaning against a stronger rupee — buying dollars is easier than spending reserves. But the same tilt shows up in the float, 0.83 against 0.52, when nobody was stepping in. The authors cannot explain it.

recall.q: The rupee swung 7.4 percent a year during the 2009–11 float. Why do the authors expect a float today to be calmer?
recall.a: Two things changed. Back then the rupee had no anchor, because the RBI was not targeting inflation; today it targets 4 percent. And the market is far deeper — daily trading has gone from about $40 billion to about $140 billion, which absorbs shocks better.

cards.title: 1,213 people took up West Africa's diaspora citizenship
cards.body: Benin, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau and Sierra Leone all offer citizenship to descendants of Africans taken in the transatlantic slave trade. Over seven years, the four schemes granted 1,213 citizenships in total. They are chasing the same people, at four different prices.

sections.text: Diaspora here means people of African descent living abroad, whose ancestors were shipped out of this coast. The historical case is strong: a passport restores a tie that was broken on purpose. The money case is not. The 1,213 figure comes from the Migration Policy Institute. There is no central register, so the real number may be higher. But big, steady investment has not followed.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Ghana's "Year of Return", 2019 — lifted tourism, and Ghana now calls its diaspora a "17th region"
Spike Lee: a Benin citizen and public ambassador for its scheme
Fees, ancestry tests and political rights differ in all four countries

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Returnees bring money, business networks, skills and tourism, so the prize is real. But four pitches, each with its own price and its own ancestry test, turn one shared inheritance into a bidding war between neighbours.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Whether ECOWAS — the West African bloc — sets one shared framework for citizenship, residency, investment and heritage tourism. The African Union has made reparations a top political priority, and a UN committee says states are legally obliged to consider reparations for the slave trade. The idea is growing. The schemes selling it are not.

recall.q: Four countries run their own diaspora citizenship schemes. Why is that a weakness rather than four times the reach?
recall.a: They share one history and largely the same pool of descendants, but each sets its own fees, ancestry tests and rights. So they compete against each other instead of offering one credible door in — the job a shared ECOWAS framework would do.

cards.title: Indian households are spending more on wants than needs
cards.body: A household spending report published on 5 September 2026 shows Indian money moving toward things people want, not things they need. The basics did not shrink. The extras just grew faster.

sections.text:
Non-essential spending — things a household chooses rather than must buy — grew faster than everything else. Alcohol and tobacco led every category. Personal care and miscellaneous goods also rose sharply, and services took a bigger share of total consumption than before.

Food spending did not fall. It grew too, with some food groups rising faster than others. So this is not a trade-off. Both baskets got bigger; the non-essential one got bigger faster.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The mix matters more than the total. More money going to services, and to goods a household picks rather than must buy, changes what companies stock and what India's consumption growth is actually made of.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: The direction is clear; the size is not. Spending in rupees rises whether households bought more or the same basket simply cost more — a spending table cannot tell the two apart. Watch whether the alcohol and tobacco lead holds over more quarters.

recall.q: Food spending rose in this data too. So what is the shift the report describes?
recall.a: A change in the mix, not a trade-off. Essential and non-essential spending both grew, but non-essentials — led by alcohol and tobacco, with personal care goods and services behind them — grew faster and took a larger share of the total.

cards.title: Gold and foreign trips: $120bn, near India's oil bill
cards.body: India's economy grew 7.8% last quarter. A day later the prime minister asked people to cut foreign holidays, weddings abroad and gold buying. Those habits need about $120 billion of foreign currency a year — close to India's whole oil import bill. The ask is not to spend less. It is to spend at home.

sections.text:
On September 1, from a summit in Bishkek, Narendra Modi asked Indians to skip holidays abroad, weddings abroad and gold they do not need. Data the day before showed 7.8% growth, above the Reserve Bank of India's forecast of about 7%.

Gold hit a record value in FY26 on high prices, not on more metal. Economist Sujan Hajra says the point is where the money goes, not how much is spent. A holiday inside India still pays Indian airlines, hotels and taxis. Gold money moved into deposits or funds keeps total savings the same size — it only changes what they pay for.

sections.label: The numbers
items: GDP: up 7.8% in the first quarter of FY27 — ₹81.36 lakh crore, from ₹75.46 lakh crore a year earlier
Gold: about 721 tonnes, worth nearly $72 billion, imported in FY26
Travel abroad: $47-50 billion (₹4-4.5 lakh crore) for about 33 million travellers in 2025
Foreign currency reserves: about $728 billion in February 2026, about $691 billion by May

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text:
Gold sits oddly in the national accounts. Buying it counts towards GDP but adds nothing to what the country can make. In one 2015 quarter, gold spending jumped 45% from a year earlier; without valuables and gaps in the data, growth would have been 6.34%, not 7.4%.

Cutting gold and travel by 10% would free about $12 billion, roughly 0.3% of GDP. Too small to move the growth path, Hajra says, but "meaningful for the current account and the rupee" — the gap between money coming into the country and money going out. Nothing is banned; the appeal came with a "wed in India" push.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Bigger forces pull the other way. Foreign investors have taken nearly $30 billion out of Indian shares in 2026. An Iran-linked spike pushed Brent crude towards $105 a barrel. And the current account deficit is put near $84 billion for the year.

recall.q: The appeal is not asking Indians to spend less. So what is it asking?
recall.a: To spend the same money inside India instead of abroad. A holiday in India still pays Indian airlines, hotels and taxis; gold money put into deposits or funds keeps total savings the same size and only changes what they pay for.

cards.title: Alzheimer's gene scores fail outside European ancestry
cards.body: A genetic risk score for Alzheimer's, built from European DNA, predicted nothing in people of African ancestry. A model built from many ancestries at once fixed that — and it matched real brain damage, not just diagnosis labels.
cards.evidence: single study · n=19,398 and n=2,559 · US cohorts · diagnosis, cognitive tests, spinal fluid, autopsy

sections.text:
Add up thousands of tiny genetic differences across a person's whole genome, give each one a weight, and you get a single number: their inherited risk of Alzheimer's disease. It is called a polygenic risk score. In this study, the standard version of that number predicted nothing for participants of African ancestry.

Not less well. Nothing.

The reason is in how the scores are built. They come from genome-wide association studies — huge projects that scan the DNA of thousands of people and pick out the small genetic differences linked to a disease. Those databases have been overwhelmingly European. Genes vary a little from one population to another, because populations have different histories. So a score built on European patterns can miss badly in someone of African or Asian descent. A 2016 study had already shown that drop in accuracy. This team asked whether newer, more diverse data could close it.
