Meri Okorie, Shea Andrews and colleagues at UC San Francisco built three scores from the same pool of global genetic data. The first used European data only. The second poured every group's data into one pile. The third — the cross-ancestry score — analyzed the groups side by side and adjusted how much weight each genetic variant should carry, based on the effects those groups shared.

The third design was the one that held up. The European-only score did well for European participants, did worse for Admixed American participants — people whose ancestry mixes Indigenous American, European and African lines — and failed outright for African-ancestry participants. The cross-ancestry score predicted best in every group. Among African-ancestry participants, a higher score came with 71 percent higher odds of an Alzheimer's diagnosis.

Then the harder test. A score can match a diagnosis label without matching the disease, so the researchers checked it against the body. Higher cross-ancestry scores went with worse memory, worse language and worse executive function — the mental skills of working memory, flexible thinking and self-control. They went with lower amyloid-beta 42 in the cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid around the brain and spine. When that protein drops there, it means it is clumping into plaques inside the brain instead. And in autopsy and brain-scan data, the highest scorers were more likely to land in the most severe categories of brain damage.

Same biology, then, showing up the same way. What had been missing was never in the people the old score failed. It was in the data the score was built from.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text:
The three scores were tested in two groups of older adults living in the United States. From the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project: 19,398 people — 7,111 with an Alzheimer's diagnosis, 12,287 cognitively normal. From the Health and Aging Brain Study–Health Disparities: 2,559 more. Both groups included people of European, Admixed American and African descent.

A step called ancestry normalization kept the scores scaled fairly across different genetic backgrounds. Every analysis adjusted for age, sex and APOE — a gene variant already known to raise Alzheimer's risk strongly on its own. Controlling for APOE is what shows whether the rest of the genome is doing any work.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text:
The test groups had no South or East Asian participants, so how the cross-ancestry score performs for them is simply unknown. Everyone tested lived in the United States; the same score might behave differently where diet, environment and daily life differ.

The researchers are also plain that these scores explain only a small part of a person's total Alzheimer's risk. Age, sex, rare genes and environment all interact to decide who actually gets the disease, and this study did not look at how environment might change genetic risk.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: When a prediction fails for a whole group, suspect the tool before you suspect the biology.

recall.q: The European-built score failed completely for African-ancestry participants. What made the cross-ancestry score different from simply pooling every group's data into one pile?
recall.a: Pooling only merges the groups. The cross-ancestry score analyzed the groups side by side and adjusted how much weight each genetic variant carries, based on the effects those groups shared. It predicted best in every group — and among African-ancestry participants, a higher score came with 71 percent higher odds of an Alzheimer's diagnosis.

cards.title: Would you want your child to be the next Confucius?
cards.body: East Asia honours Confucius as the teacher for ten thousand generations. His own life was poor, unstable and mostly ignored. It is the exact life a loving parent would beg a child not to choose.

sections.text:
A child announces the plan at dinner: I want to become a modern-day Confucius.

The parents do not ask what they would study, or what they hope to give the world. They ask the practical things. How will you make a living? Can philosophy support you? Why not medicine, or law, or technology — fields with a steadier future?

The questions are not cruel. Education costs more every year. The job market is crowded. Success is usually measured in income or social standing. Wanting your child to take the safe road is one of the ordinary shapes of love.

Now the odd part. Confucius sits near the centre of Chinese history. His ideas shaped education, ethics and political life across East Asia for more than two thousand years. Chinese students study the Confucian classics — the core texts of his tradition — at every level of school. Institutes carrying his name teach the language and culture around the world.

History built that Confucius afterwards. The man himself was born into a poor family with no political standing. His father died early. He grew up in a feudal world, where your family's rank decided what protection you had, and that loss left him exposed.

He held small government posts, then turned to teaching and to changing how rulers govern. He wanted office and was refused it for most of his life. He travelled from state to state with his students, trying to talk rulers into his ideas. Mostly he was ignored or sent away. Once the group ran out of food on the road and came close to dying of hunger and illness.

The title he carries now — teacher for ten thousand generations — was given by the future. Measured the way a parent measures, his own lifetime was a failing career. Unstable, uncertain, with no sign that any of it would last.

So the wish and the warning sit at the same table. We hope the world keeps producing people like him. Almost nobody hopes it will be their own child. The safe-career question gets asked from inside the life, while everything is still only risk. The honour gets handed out much later, by people who never had to live it.

sections.label: Steelman
sections.text: The worried parent is not the villain here. From inside a life, you cannot tell a future teacher of ten thousand generations from a person who simply fails. At twenty, the two look the same. The parents are protecting their child against the far more common one.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The honour arrives two thousand years late. The risk arrives at dinner.

recall.q: Confucius is honoured across East Asia, yet almost no parent would want their child to live his actual life. What explains the gap?
recall.a: The honour is hindsight. In his own lifetime he was poor and fatherless, held only small posts, was turned away by ruler after ruler, and once nearly starved on the road with his students. The reputation was given by the future; the risk had to be lived through first.

cards.title: Postpartum psychosis: half the risk is inherited
cards.body: Swedish records for 1.6 million mothers put the inherited share of postpartum psychosis risk at 55 percent, close to bipolar disorder. That moves it away from the old story of a mind breaking under the stress of childbirth. And the gene that stood out most is not a brain gene at all. It controls how the body makes cholesterol.
cards.evidence: single study · Swedish registry: 1.6M mothers, 2,514 cases · sequencing: 198 then 461 cases vs 2,013 and 4,610 controls

sections.text:
Sweden records every birth. Between 1980 and 2017, more than 1.6 million women there had a first child. For 2,514 of them, 0.15 percent, the weeks after the birth brought mania, severe depression, confusion, and psychosis: losing contact with reality through hallucinations or delusions. It comes on fast, it puts mother and baby in danger, and it usually means hospital care at once.

Postpartum psychosis has long been read as a reaction to the shock of childbirth. A team led by Seulgi Jung and Behrang Mahjani at Mount Sinai tested that sideways, through the sisters and cousins of these mothers. If closer relatives carry more of the risk, the risk is inherited. Their number came to 55 percent. More than half of who gets it and who does not traces back to genes, close to what is seen for bipolar disorder.

Then they asked what kind of genes. Common variants are the ordinary spelling differences in DNA that huge numbers of people carry, each nudging risk a little. In whole-genome data from 198 affected mothers and 2,013 matched controls, common variants explained about 45.6 percent of the risk. Near 55, but short of it. The gap is where rarer mutations live.

So the team hunted for rare breaks: mutations that stop a gene from making a working protein at all. Comparing 461 women who had postpartum psychosis with 4,610 who had not, they found these breaks piled up in genes that normally tolerate almost no damage. About 81 genes carry risk, they estimate. One stood out, and it was not a brain gene: HMGCR, which holds the instructions for a key enzyme the body uses to make cholesterol.

The cholesterol thread is not new. A 2017 review pooling many studies found changed cholesterol levels in people going through a first psychotic episode. A 2013 study found immune trouble in first episodes of postpartum psychosis. Here both threads met. Many of the top risk genes for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia turned up again, and so did genes tied to autoimmune illness, where the immune system attacks the body: rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, Crohn's disease. HMGCR itself is a top risk gene for both schizophrenia and rheumatoid arthritis. In large medical biobanks, its broken copies also tracked with vascular dementia. Whatever it does to the brain, it is not doing it only after birth.

Mahjani is careful about the gene. It "should not be read as 'the postpartum psychosis gene'", he says. It is one of many, and the condition is highly polygenic: built from many genes, each adding a small amount. The heavier claim is the 55 percent. It says the weakness is biological and already there, and childbirth only sets it off. This is not a character giving way under stress.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: The gene samples are small for this kind of work, 198 cases and then 461, and almost all of European ancestry, so the picture may not hold in other populations. Hospitals also define postpartum psychosis differently from place to place, and the registry often lacked the end dates of episodes, so nobody could say how long they lasted. Most important: the team did not separate women having a first psychiatric episode from women already living with something like bipolar disorder. Some of this may be the genetics of severe mental illness in general, not of the weeks after birth.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The trigger arrives with the baby. The vulnerability was there long before.

recall.q: Common gene variants explained about 45.6 percent of the risk, but family patterns pointed to 55 percent. What did the researchers do with that gap?
recall.a: They read the gap as room for rarer genetics and went looking for mutations that break a gene outright. Those breaks were unusually common in women with postpartum psychosis, pointing to about 81 risk genes, with the cholesterol enzyme gene HMGCR standing out.

cards.title: The Dutch moved 86 tonnes of gold. Most never moved.
cards.body: The Dutch central bank pulled 86 tonnes of gold out of the US and Canada this year and placed it with the Bank of England. It pointed to rising tension between countries. But only about a third of that gold was ever carried anywhere. The rest was sold in New York and bought again in London.

sections.text:
De Nederlandsche Bank said it wanted gold it could reach fast in a crisis, and cited "increasing geopolitical unrest". Its governor, Olaf Sleijpen, said he expects the reserves will never actually be needed.

Most of the gold never crossed the Atlantic. About 59 tonnes were sold in New York and the same amount bought in London: a swap on paper, nothing shipped. Just over 27 tonnes physically moved from North America to the Dutch town of Zeist, and a similar amount from Zeist on to London.

The Dutch are not first. France pulled its reserves back from the US earlier this year.

sections.label: The numbers
items: 86 tonnes shifted between March and August, out of about 313 the Dutch held in the US and Canada
216 tonnes brought home by Germany's Bundesbank in the years to 2016 — 111 from New York, 105 from Paris
1,000 tonnes a year — average central bank gold buying over the past four years, double the 500-tonne average of the decade before
400,000 bars, worth more than £200bn, sit under the Bank of England — still the most popular place to store gold

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: Joseph Cavatoni of the World Gold Council says war and trade tension are not the top reason. Inflation, interest rates and sitting somewhere you can trade fast count too, and he gets no sense of "impending doom". London wins because it is the trading centre: if you must sell in a hurry, the buyers are there. Keeping gold at home is not free either — Goldman Sachs notes the security, audit and insurance costs, which hit small central banks hardest.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: Central bank buying is one main reason the gold price keeps climbing. It passed $5,000 an ounce in January before easing. Goldman Sachs forecasts $4,900 a troy ounce by the end of 2026 — about $300 above the August level.

recall.q: The Dutch moved 86 tonnes of gold to London. How much of it actually travelled, and how did the rest get there?
recall.a: Only a bit over 27 tonnes physically moved, going first to Zeist in the Netherlands and then on to London. The other 59 or so tonnes were sold in New York and the same amount bought in London — a paper swap, with no gold crossing the ocean.
